For this branch, direct differentiation gives ∂L/∂h = δαe, ∂L/∂e = δαh, and ∂L/∂g = δ sigmoid(g)(h·e), where α=softplus(g), δ=∂L/∂s. At α=0.01, g≈−4.60 and sigmoid(g)≈0.00995: small embeddings suppress embedding gradients, while their product also suppresses gate learning. Assuming independent, zero-mean coordinates with standard deviations σh, σe, residual-score RMS is α√d σhσe. Increasing dimension increases this RMS only at fixed coordinate variance; with both standard deviations proportional to d⁻¹ᐟ², it decreases as d⁻¹ᐟ². These are analytical implications, not measured benchmark results.

Tiny gradients do not necessarily imply tiny Adam updates: adaptive normalization can largely cancel consistent gradient scaling, until epsilon, noise, or regularization matters. An explicit squared penalty λ‖E‖² contributes 2λE; compare this against task gradients, especially for infrequent items. Full-table penalties can shrink embeddings even when their rows receive no task signal. Unsquared norm penalties behave differently, so inspect the exact expression and reduction. Adam’s coupled L2 and AdamW’s decoupled shrinkage are distinct; applying both compounds regularization. [AdamW paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05101).

Avoid multiplying several tiny initial scales: calibrate random embedding variance and gate jointly against baseline-score RMS. Alternatively, use a moderate nonzero gate, one random factor, and one zero factor; the zero factor receives initial task gradients. Both factors zero produce no task gradient. ReZero’s zero gate instead relies on a nonzero branch output to learn its gate. [ReZero paper](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v161/bachlechner21a.html). Track per-category gate/norm trajectories, task-versus-penalty gradients, actual update/parameter ratios, residual/base score RMS and positive–negative margins, rank changes, and validation HR@10 with the residual ablated.
